title: Payers are using AI to write coverage policy. Market access teams need to get there first.
summary: AI-drafted payer policies may be finalized before launch, and they can come out more restrictive than intended. That changes when and how market access teams engage.
body: A quiet shift is underway on the payer side. MMIT's 2026 market access outlook notes that health plans increasingly use AI to draft medical policies, evaluate utilization trends, and design formularies and utilization management. Because these models lean on clinical trial inclusion criteria, the resulting policies can end up more restrictive than the payer actually intended.

The timing matters as much as the content. If an AI-assisted policy is drafted before approval, the window to influence it closes earlier than most launch plans assume. MMIT's experts recommend identifying the most influential payers and engaging them well ahead of launch, with access planning starting as early as Phase 1 or 2.

This lands on top of an already tight environment. MMIT data cited in the same piece shows new-to-market blocks rising from roughly half of U.S. covered lives a few years ago to almost two-thirds by 2025. IQVIA's July 2026 market access view adds accumulators, maximizers, and IRA and 340B uncertainty to the list of pressures on net revenue.

What this means for MA&R analytics teams: payer segmentation and policy monitoring can no longer be quarterly exercises. Teams that can quickly compare a draft policy against trial criteria, covered lives, and historical payer behavior will be the ones who shape the outcome rather than react to it.

One caution. Industry research from Day One Strategy finds that AI access in pharma is outpacing real adoption, and that data quality and governance decide whether AI investments pay off. The same holds here: AI-ready payer data (clean hierarchies, current policy text, reliable lives counts) is the foundation, not an afterthought.

title: Drug prior authorization is becoming digital infrastructure. That is a data opportunity for access teams.
summary: CMS's proposed rule on prior authorization for drugs pushes payers toward electronic workflows, faster decisions, and public reporting. The result is a new, structured data stream that access analytics and AI can actually use.
body: In April 2026 CMS proposed its Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs rule. As Fierce Healthcare reported, it would require payers in Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and ACA exchange plans to decide drug prior authorization requests within 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for urgent ones, publicly report approval, denial, and appeal metrics, and move to FHIR-based electronic workflows.

A contributor piece in AJMC frames this well: CMS is shifting from trimming administrative burden to rebuilding prior authorization as digital infrastructure. It extends reform to drugs under both the medical and pharmacy benefit, asks for more specific denial reasons, and notes that contracts signed in 2026 will govern performance during the 2027 compliance period.

The scale explains the urgency. AJMC cites KFF data showing Medicare Advantage insurers made 52.8 million prior authorization determinations in 2024 and denied 7.7%. Meanwhile, MMIT's 2026 outlook expects payers and pharmacies to use AI to reduce administrative work and speed prior authorization reviews.

Put those together and the picture changes for manufacturers. Prior authorization has been one of the least visible steps in the patient journey, usually seen through hub data, field anecdotes, and lagging claims. Standardized electronic transactions, deadlines, and published payer metrics create a cleaner, more consistent signal about where and why patients get stuck.

What it means for MA&R analytics teams: start building the baseline now. Map turnaround and denial patterns by payer and benefit type, connect them to payer hierarchy and covered lives, and line them up with patient services and specialty pharmacy data. When the reporting arrives, the teams with a clean baseline will be the ones who can tell real access improvement from noise, and who are ready to put AI on top of data that finally holds together.

title: HTA bodies have not banned AI in evidence dossiers. They have made it auditable.
summary: NICE, the EU HTA Coordination Group and Canada's Drug Agency now share one expectation for AI in evidence submissions: disclose it, keep a human accountable, and show the validation. For MA&R teams, that turns AI use into a documentation and governance job.
body: Over the past two years, the rules for using AI in health technology assessment submissions have taken shape, and they point the same way. None of the major bodies prohibits AI. Each one makes the manufacturer answerable for it. An October analysis from Eularis made exactly that point in its headline: nobody has banned AI in HTA submissions, but everybody has made you answerable for it.

NICE set the template in its August 2024 position statement. Declare any AI use and explain why it was chosen. Keep a capable person in the loop. Validate the method and report risks such as bias. NICE also asks that established, more explainable methods come first, with less transparent approaches presented as supplementary.

The EU followed. On 15 July 2026 the HTA Coordination Group adopted general principles for AI use in Joint Clinical Assessment dossiers. As Cytel summarizes them, developers stay fully responsible for the evidence and conclusions, no step should be fully automated, and each meaningful AI use must be documented with the tool, version, developer and purpose. Prompts should be retained and available on request. In Canada, Smart & Biggar reports that Canada's Drug Agency issued guidance in July 2026 on AI methods used to extract variables from unstructured data for real-world evidence. It says AI should be used only when clearly justified and should not yet replace well-established approaches.

The practical message is that the burden has moved from the method to the record. An AI-assisted literature screen or an extraction table is acceptable only if you can show what the tool did, who checked it, and how it was validated. That record has to exist before the dossier is written. It cannot be rebuilt afterwards.

For MA&R analytics teams, this is a data governance task. Treat AI-assisted evidence work like any other controlled data pipeline: version the tools, log prompts and outputs, capture human review sign-offs, and store validation results next to the analysis. The same discipline will strengthen US payer value dossiers, even where no rule requires it yet. Teams that build the audit trail now will move faster as JCA scope expands to orphan medicines in January 2028.

title: AI agents are reaching field access teams. Governance has not caught up.
summary: AI agents built for field reimbursement work are now on the market, while most pharma companies still lack fully operational AI governance. MA&R analytics should set the data and oversight rules before the agents start talking to provider offices.
body: Field reimbursement work is starting to get its own AI agents. On October 7, Fierce Healthcare reported that Infinitus launched a suite of AI agents for pharma sales reps and field reimbursement managers. On the access side, the agents answer questions about prior authorization status, claims and reimbursement, and help onboard provider offices with approved access materials. The company frames it as augmenting field teams, not replacing them. Fierce notes there are no performance metrics, pricing or named customers yet.

The direction matters more than any one vendor. Field access teams sit where payer rules meet the provider office. The questions they handle every day, such as where a PA stands or why a claim was denied, depend on data that already flows through hubs, specialty pharmacies and payer portals. An agent that answers those questions is only as good as that data and the rules around it.

That is where the industry still looks thin. ZS's 2027 CDIO Outlook Survey, released October 6, found that 56% of respondents report measurable AI outcomes in commercial sales and marketing, up from 47% a year earlier. But 55% of organizations are still defining or rolling out AI governance, and only 17% say it is fully operational enterprise-wide. ZS also found that 72% of its "AI value leaders" rank data for AI as mission-critical, versus 46% of other organizations.

Put those together and the risk is clear. Agents that talk to provider offices about coverage and reimbursement are a compliance-sensitive use case. If governance lags deployment, the first problems will show up as inconsistent answers, unclear escalation paths and interaction records no one can audit.

What it means for MA&R analytics teams: get ahead of the field. Define the source of truth for PA and claim status before an agent starts quoting it. Agree on what an agent may say, when it hands off to a person, and how every interaction is logged. Plan to measure outcomes such as time to therapy and abandonment, not just call volume. If analytics does not set those rules, the vendor contract will.

title: 340B is becoming a claim-level data problem. Access analytics teams should build for it now.
summary: HRSA approved 10 manufacturers for its revised 340B rebate pilot and CMS opened a Part D 340B claims repository on the same day. Both run on claim-level data, and the timelines make automated, auditable matching a requirement.
body: On October 1, two federal 340B data efforts moved forward on the same day. HRSA approved 10 manufacturers for its revised 340B Rebate Model Pilot, set to begin January 1, 2027, according to AHA News. CMS opened its Medicare Part D 340B claims repository for voluntary submissions. The AHA says it is considering all available options to stop the pilot, so legal risk has not gone away.

The common thread is claim-level data. Epstein Becker Green's summary of the HRSA notice lists 11 required pharmacy claim fields and, new this year, 12 medical claim fields. Covered entities submit within 45 days of dispense, and manufacturers must pay or deny a rebate within 10 calendar days of a complete submission. CMS describes its repository as a test of whether covered-entity data can reliably identify 340B units to exclude from Part D inflation rebate calculations. Testing data will not be used for that purpose yet.

A 10-day clock leaves little room for manual review. Matching submitted claims to rebate invoices, catching duplicates, and making a pay-or-deny call at that pace will push teams toward automated matching and anomaly detection. IntegriChain argues manufacturers need consistent duplicate discount logic across Medicaid, commercial, and Medicare, with 340B claim validation built into the rebate cycle rather than run after it.

The catch is that every denial will be challenged. Hospitals are already contesting the model in public and in court. Any automated or AI-assisted matching has to be documented, reproducible, and easy to explain to a covered entity or a regulator. A model score on its own is not a defensible reason to deny a rebate.

What it means for MA&R analytics teams: treat 340B claims as a core data asset, not a side file owned by contracting. Build one claim-level foundation that joins 340B submissions to Medicaid, commercial, and Medicare rebate data, with NDC-11 and pharmacy identifiers mastered. Start with clear matching rules, add machine learning only where it lifts match rates and can be audited, and report the gross-to-net impact by channel. That work pays off whether or not the pilot survives.

title: Wholesalers are using AI to read demand earlier. Trade analytics teams should not be the last to see it.
summary: Cencora is piloting an AI tool that flags demand shifts from ordering patterns, while the channel itself is changing under net pricing, IRA and 340B. Manufacturer trade analytics needs its own channel data in order before the distributor sees the shift first.
body: Pharmaceutical Commerce reported on October 14 that Cencora has rolled out an AI tool to a handful of its buyers. It flags demand shifts by comparing historical forecasts with incoming ordering patterns, explains its reasoning, and lets buyers ask what drove a spike. Cencora says early results show a 10% forecasting improvement on a limited set of SKUs.

The more telling detail is what the tool works without. Cencora's Matt Sample noted that the distributor does not receive the point-of-sale demand data that consumer supply chains rely on. The gain came from putting forecasts, ordering history, and ERP data in one place, work buyers used to do by hand in spreadsheets. Cencora is also building knowledge graphs that link manufacturers to FDA actions and other risk factors to spot shortage patterns.

The channel these models learn from is also moving. Drug Channels Institute's 2026 wholesaler outlook describes a shift toward a net pricing drug channel, with manufacturers cutting list prices on more than 30 brands. It also expects IRA negotiated prices for selected Part B drugs, starting in 2028, to shift purchasing volume toward large hospitals and 340B covered entities. Past ordering patterns will be a weaker guide to future demand.

Speakers at LogiPharma USA 2026 made the sequencing point plainly. Pfizer's Gisele Fahmi put a standard process and trusted master data ahead of any AI, and said AI can clean data faster than humans but cannot connect departments. Johnson & Johnson's Marcio Alves da Silva added that teams must be able to explain why a model reached its answer.

For MA&R analytics teams, the lesson is practical. Trade teams already hold the signals that matter: 852 inventory, 867 sell-through, specialty pharmacy dispense data, and chargeback feeds. If a distributor spots a demand shift before the brand's own trade analytics does, that is a data integration gap, not a tooling gap. Reconcile product and customer master data across these feeds first. Then build exception alerts the trade and forecasting teams can trust and explain, and track channel mix by class of trade as IRA and 340B changes take hold.

title: Market access teams report AI efficiency gains. Very few can prove the return.
summary: A new peer-reviewed survey of European market access leaders finds AI is saving time, but only 9% of adopters report a clearly measurable return. The gap is data and measurement, not models.
body: Most AI surveys in pharma look at R&D or the enterprise as a whole. A study published in September in Global and Regional Health Technology Assessment looks at market access specifically. Researchers at ProductLife Group surveyed 50 European market access executives and senior leaders. Overall, 44% reported formal AI deployment in their organization. Size mattered: 85% of large companies had deployed AI, compared with 28% of medium and 32% of small companies.

Among the 22 companies using AI, market access was the function most affected, cited by 59%. And 86% reported efficiency gains. But only 9%, two companies, reported a clearly positive and measurable return. Another 55% saw a return they found hard to measure, and 32% had seen no tangible results yet.

The barriers will sound familiar. Among companies using AI in market access, lack of training data and difficulty integrating with existing systems were each cited by 45%. Regulatory acceptance of AI-based evidence was cited by 36%. Some respondents reported trouble justifying AI models to regulators or payers, and some saw biased or inaccurate recommendations affecting pricing and reimbursement. The authors are clear that the sample is small and may lean toward AI-engaged professionals.

ZS's 2027 CDIO Outlook Survey, released in October, points the same way at enterprise level. It reports that 56% of organizations saw measurable AI outcomes in commercial sales and marketing, up from 47%. Among its 'AI value leaders', 72% rank data for AI as mission-critical, versus 46% of other organizations. Only 17% say AI governance is fully operational across the enterprise.

What it means for MA&R analytics teams: efficiency is not the same as value, and leadership will soon ask for the difference. Pick the metric before the pilot starts: analyst hours on payer policy review, time to refresh a coverage view, forecast error, pull-through. Baseline it now. Fix the data layer first, because that is where these projects stall: payer hierarchy mapping, formulary-to-claims linkage, clean contract terms. Keep a human checkpoint on anything that touches pricing, contracting, or a payer submission. The teams that can show the number will keep the funding.

title: Medicare will delink PBM pay from drug prices in 2028. Contract analytics needs a rebuild now.
summary: A CMS proposed rule would limit Part D PBMs to flat service fees and require full rebate pass-through from 2028. Access analytics teams should start modeling what that does to contract value and gross-to-net.
body: On October 16, CMS released a proposed rule implementing the Medicare provisions of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2026. According to a McDermott client alert, PBMs serving Part D plans could earn only bona fide service fees, defined as the cost of a service plus a reasonable markup. Manufacturer rebates would have to be fully passed through to the plan sponsor, meaning 100% of their gross economic value. The requirements apply to plan years starting January 1, 2028. Comments are due December 15.

Healthcare Dive reports that those fees could not depend on a drug's price, the rebates it generates, or its formulary placement. PBMs would also report annually to sponsors and CMS on what was dispensed, where, and what revenue the PBM kept.

For manufacturers, this goes to the core of how Part D contracts are valued. Fees tied to list price and rebate size have long been part of the math behind formulary deals. If the rule is finalized as proposed, the conversation moves toward net cost and access outcomes, and plans will hold far more data on both.

Data and AI are the other half of the story. At the PBMI conference, as reported by Managed Healthcare Executive, speakers said transparency alone is not enough and called for actionable data and real-time technology. Dana McCormick of AMCP said technology could help fit population-level utilization management policies to individual patients, and speakers expect employers to adopt AI over the next five years. McCormick also cautioned that more transparency does not automatically mean more value.

What this means for MA&R analytics teams: build Part D contract scenarios under delinked compensation now, covering rebate tiers, fee exposure, and gross-to-net accruals. Inventory every contract term tied to WAC or rebate percentage. AI can speed up the reading of contract language and invoice reconciliation, but the assumptions need human owners. And plan for payers who will arrive at 2028 negotiations with cleaner data and sharper utilization management tools.

title: Medicare's GLOBE model is final and narrow. The international price data work is not.
summary: CMS finalized a much smaller most-favored-nation model for Part B, but its benchmark design rewards manufacturers that can defend net prices by country. That is a data foundation job before it is an AI job.
body: CMS finalized the GLOBE model on September 30. It is a mandatory Medicare Part B model that compares U.S. prices for certain drugs against prices in 19 reference countries, adjusted for GDP on a purchasing-power basis. According to Skadden, collection of voluntary manufacturer-submitted international net price data begins January 1, 2027.

The final rule is far narrower than the proposal. Health Affairs Forefront reports that coverage fell to about 3 percent of eligible Part B drug spending, down from about 54 percent, and projected federal savings dropped to $440 million from $11.9 billion. Orphan-only drugs, cell and gene therapies and plasma-derived products are now excluded, and manufacturers in the Medicaid GENEROUS model can receive waivers. CMS estimates as few as four manufacturers may be covered. PhRMA sued about a week after finalization.

Narrow does not mean irrelevant. The benchmark design matters more than today's drug list. By default, CMS estimates the lowest country-level price, largely from public and list prices. A manufacturer can instead submit volume-weighted net prices, which Skadden notes must account for discounts, free goods, chargebacks and rebates. That option only helps if the company can produce clean, defensible net prices by country and by unit.

This is where AI belongs, and where it does not. Model N, a pricing software vendor, argues that spreadsheets cannot keep up with granular, constantly changing international pricing data. I agree with the diagnosis. In my view, AI can help monitor reference-country price changes, flag unit and pack-size mismatches, and draft scenario summaries. It cannot fix a net price that was never reconciled across affiliates. The inputs have to be governed first.

For MA&R analytics teams, the practical step is a GLOBE readiness view, even if no current product qualifies: Part B spend against the $100 million threshold, the exclusion logic, and an international price file mapped to U.S. units with the GDP(PPP) adjustment. Build it with global pricing and legal, keep an audit trail, and treat the default lowest-price benchmark as the downside case in gross-to-net forecasts. The models will keep changing. The data discipline carries over.

title: Patient support AI is moving from efficiency to accountability. Hub data needs to keep up.
summary: IQVIA's look-back on 2026 patient support says programs are now judged on time to therapy, and that AI in benefits verification and patient finance faces real scrutiny. Access analytics teams should own the measurement.
body: Patient support is changing what it gets judged on. In an October look-back on its 2026 predictions, IQVIA's patient support leaders say programs are shifting from activity counts to access progress: how quickly a patient moves from prescription to therapy. The metrics they name are benefits verification turnaround, prior authorization submission and resolution, and where patients hit barriers.

AI is taking on the routine work. IQVIA describes intake, documentation, status updates and appropriate self-service moving to technology, while people keep judgment, exceptions, relationships and escalation. The next step it describes is proactive support, using predictive signals, next-best actions and program data to find barriers early.

The harder message is about scrutiny. IQVIA says data use, governance and integrity in benefits verification and AI-driven patient finance are under closer review, and that buyers want evidence of how automation performs across their own patient population and payer mix before they change staffing. It calls this a move from AI efficiency to AI accountability. It also expects PBM transparency changes to turn patient support into an analytics layer for benefit verification, deductible reconciliation, appeals and payer-level reporting.

Manufacturers are also pulling more of this closer. A Pharmaceutical Commerce roundtable, citing a Cardinal Health survey, reports that 39% of executives felt leadership pressure to move hub functions in-house, up from 28% in 2024. The same piece cites IQVIA data that an average of 35% of first-year prescriptions were filled across 99 novel medicines. That is the gap all of this is meant to close.

For MA&R analytics teams, the hub is now a data product, not a monthly vendor report. Build a time-to-therapy view at the case level, cut by payer, channel and plan type. Ask hub partners for stage timestamps and reason codes in a defined schema. Set baselines before any AI rollout so performance can be checked by payer mix and patient segment. And keep an audit trail for automated benefits and affordability decisions. When compliance asks how the automation performed, the answer should already be in the data.

title: Physicians now check AI before they prescribe. Access evidence has to be readable by machines.
summary: New Bain and IQVIA research shows AI tools are becoming a regular stop in clinical decisions. For MA&R, the question is whether HEOR and real-world evidence actually show up in those answers.
body: Bain published a brief on October 26 with a number access teams should notice. The share of US physicians who rank AI among their top three sources for prescribing decisions rose from 3% in December 2024 to 20% in June 2026, according to Bain's surveys. About one-third say their organization uses AI clinical decision support tools such as UpToDate and OpenEvidence, and more than half of those users consult them multiple times a day.

IQVIA sees the same shift from the question side. Its 2026 survey of 23,769 physicians across 34 markets found 80% used at least one AI tool. In an analysis of more than 2,000 HCP prompts from France, Germany and the UK, guidelines were the largest topic, followed by treatment selection and diagnosis, and almost one-third of topics were patient-specific. IQVIA also notes that payers may bring their own questions to these tools.

Most of the commentary frames this as a brand visibility issue. I think it is also an evidence issue for MA&R. Bain recommends evidence portfolios that cover more patient subtypes and real-world scenarios, structured so AI tools can retrieve and apply them. That is the same evidence HEOR and RWE teams build for payers and P&T committees. Precision AQ has suggested that health-system P&T committees may use AI evidence platforms as a reference point. It labels that a hypothesis, and it should be treated as one.

The risk is quiet. If a subgroup analysis or a real-world outcomes study is hard to find or hard to parse, it may simply not appear in the answer. Nobody issues a denial. The evidence just does not show up.

For MA&R analytics teams, the practical step is to start measuring. Run a fixed set of access-relevant questions, such as place in therapy, subpopulations and comparative real-world outcomes, through the major tools each quarter and log which sources get cited. Make sure published HEOR and RWE work exists in structured, indexable formats. Keep the work to evidence stewardship, correcting errors rather than promoting, with medical and compliance in the loop. AI answers are now another channel where evidence lands. Track it like one.

title: AI is making HEOR faster. The evidence says it is not yet making it truer.
summary: A new scoping review finds AI gains in health economics and outcomes research are real for extraction and screening, but unproven where the answer is a causal estimate. Access teams should split their AI work along that line.
body: A scoping review published in the Journal of Health Economics and Outcomes Research on October 15, titled "Faster but Not Truer," mapped 2,476 PubMed records on AI in HEOR from 2010 to 2025. Annual output grew from 29 records to 852. Only 17 records, or 0.7%, were validation studies.

The review finds gains where there is a ground truth to check against. In one cited study of 12,814 extractions across 107 trials, Claude 3.5 reached 96.2% accuracy, human extractors 95.3%, and humans assisted by the model 97.9%. Causal questions are different. In an emulation of the PARADIGM-HF trial, which reported a hazard ratio of 0.81, a model with an AUC of 0.95 produced 0.61, while a weaker model produced 0.93. The author's conclusion: predictive performance repeatedly fails to predict evidentiary performance. He also could not document any regulator or HTA body explicitly accepting or rejecting an AI-derived endpoint.

The cost side tells a similar story. A ConnectHEOR abstract for ISPOR Europe 2026 reviewed AI-assisted deliverables and found that counting only junior analyst hours overstated the benefit in every one. Effort shifted to senior reviewers. Net economics were strongly favorable for repeatable, high-volume tasks, and much weaker for one-off, judgment-heavy work.

Komodo Health's Ashis Das, writing after ISPOR 2026, notes that AI topped ISPOR's HEOR Trends report for the first time, yet there is still no consensus on how to validate AI-generated HEOR outputs. He argues for experts making calls at defined points in the workflow, not a human check bolted on at the end.

For MA&R analytics teams, the practical move is to sort the work. Literature screening, data extraction, and payer policy abstraction have checkable answers. Automate them, sample the output, and publish measured error rates. Comparative effectiveness from claims, budget impact assumptions, and other counterfactual work need senior methodologists owning design and benchmarking results against known trial or historical estimates. Plan and budget that review time up front. It is where the real cost now sits.

title: Eight states now require a human behind AI coverage denials. Access teams should read denial data differently.
summary: A new state legislation report counts eight states that bar health insurers from relying solely on AI for adverse coverage decisions. For MA&R analytics, that turns state of residence into a variable in prior authorization and denial trends.
body: On October 27 the Transparency Coalition released its 2026 State AI Legislation Report, counting 115 new AI laws across 30 states this year. One category matters directly to market access: eight states (Alabama, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Utah and Washington) enacted laws limiting the ability of health insurers to rely solely on AI or automated systems for adverse authorization or coverage decisions.

The details differ by state. The Coalition's earlier mid-year summary notes that Alabama requires insurers to disclose AI use and have denials made by a licensed physician or health professional, effective October 1, 2026. Colorado requires decisions to reflect the individual patient's history rather than group data alone. Georgia and Utah take effect January 1, 2027. The National Law Review reports that Washington goes furthest on transparency: carriers must report to the insurance commissioner the percentage of prior authorization denials aided by AI, and Utah insurers must disclose AI use to the state insurance department.

None of this bans AI in utilization review. Payers can still use it to triage and approve. What changes is the path to a denial, which now needs a qualified human in the loop. That can affect turnaround times, denial rationale language and how often first-pass decisions hold on appeal.

The landscape is not settled. TechTimes, covering the same report, notes Congress has passed no federal AI law and a DOJ task force has been challenging state AI laws in court. State insurance rules also generally do not reach self-funded employer plans, so the effect will be uneven across a brand's covered lives.

For MA&R analytics teams, the practical step is to stop treating prior authorization and denial trends as purely payer-level. Tag hub, specialty pharmacy and PA data by patient state and plan funding type, mark each law's effective date, and watch for breaks in approval rates, time to decision and appeal overturns. Washington's AI-aided denial reporting, if made public, could become a new input to payer intelligence. Build the baseline now, before the January 2027 effective dates make before-and-after comparisons harder.

title: Part B negotiated prices land by November 30. Buy-and-bill analytics needs to be ready first.
summary: The third Medicare negotiation cycle brings Part B drugs into scope for the first time. The data signals will be fragmented, so access and trade analytics teams should build the scenario models and early-warning views now.
body: CMS is due to publish negotiated prices for the third cycle of Medicare drug price negotiation by November 30, according to Milliman. For the first time, the list includes Part B drugs. Milliman names Botox, Cimzia, Entyvio, Orencia and Xolair among them. The prices take effect January 1, 2028.

The mechanics matter more than the headline discount. Avalere Health notes that Medicare fee-for-service will pay providers 106% of the maximum fair price, replacing ASP plus 6%. Milliman adds that prices from the first two cycles reflected average list price discounts of about 60%, that ASP itself will fall as negotiated prices enter the average, and that CMS will not publish ASP for negotiated drugs. Milliman expects 340B hospitals to see the largest margin loss.

Behavior will follow margin. In an Avalere survey of more than 300 practices, reported by Managed Healthcare Executive, 92% said they were somewhat or very likely to stop stocking negotiated Part B drugs. Both Avalere and Milliman flag possible site-of-care shifts, and commercial and Medicare Advantage contracts pegged to Medicare rates or ASP that may need renegotiation.

The data will not arrive cleanly. Milliman notes that Part B claims process with a lag and that effectuation guidance for Part B is still in draft. Avalere notes it is unclear how negotiated prices will flow into Medicare Advantage benchmarks and risk adjustment. Early signals will show up first in specialty distributor sales, site-of-care mix and plan medical policy, well before they show up in claims.

For MA&R analytics teams, the work starts now. Build the scenario model with the negotiated price as a variable and flag every ASP-linked contract. Set up account-level views of ordering by site of care using trade and distribution data. AI tools can help monitor medical policy and contract language changes at scale, but the value depends on having account, contract and claims data joined before the prices publish. Keep people accountable for the assumptions.
